newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Dutch crack down on hard drugs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Dutch crack down on hard drugs.

text.p: "It's legal, but it ain't 100 percent legal," is how the John Travolta character in 1995's blockbuster movie "Pulp Fiction" describes the Dutch stance on drugs such as cannabis and marijuana.

It's a paradox that neatly sums up foreign bewilderment -- and often dismay -- at the Netherlands' policy of tolerance towards socially sensitive issues such as prostitution, soft drug use and euthanasia.

Now, however, the Netherlands' major cities are seeking to tighten up regulations governing soft drugs use after years of informal control which, some believe, has spawned a parallel underworld of crime and hard drugs trading.

In recent months the link between soft drugs and serious crime has captured the public imagination with the highly publicised trial of Dutch drugs baron Johan Verhoek, sentenced last month to six years for organised drugs smuggling.
Known as the Hakkelaar (Stutterer), Verhoek headed the "Octopus" drugs gang, so-called because its tentacles were said by prosecution witnesses to "extend to the highest levels" of society.
Since the late 1980s the gang was found to have smuggled more than 200 tonnes of cannabis into the Netherlands.
FOREIGN PRESSURE FOR REFORM
A hardening attitude at home coincides with pressure from European neighbours -- notably France -- to crack the whip.
While many other countries attempt to eliminate all forms of drug taking, the Dutch plan to bring the small-scale cannabis outlets, known as coffee shops, into the fold.
Amsterdam, eager to shrug off its image as Europe's drugs capital, is at the forefront of the changes, pledging to cut its number of coffee shops and subject the rest to strict controls.
"We had years of tolerance in the 1970s and 1980s. Now there's a moment that we accept them, but we want strict regulations," says Mirjam Otten, a spokeswoman for the Amsterdam mayor's office.
"As for soft drugs, the policy now is to give coffee shops a sort of permission."
In 1995, Amsterdam froze the number of its coffee shops at existing levels, anticipating the total would slowly dwindle from an original 350.
Last year, the clampdown was extended to include a ban on the sale of alcohol on coffee shop premises and the stepping up of police controls.
Ninety of Amsterdam's coffee shops currently run a bar. Within the year, they will have to decide whether their future lies with alcohol or drugs.
This year, for the first time, certificates will be given to those coffee shops that meet the narrower criteria.
Not everyone, however, is prepared to recognise, even covertly, the taking of soft drugs.
In Kampen, in the north of the country, the mayor threatened to resign if the council passed a motion approving the opening of a coffee shop within municipal boundaries.

In the northern city of Groningen, tougher regulations have brought the number of coffee shops down from 35 to 14. Despite this, a third of school pupils now claim to have tried soft drugs, compared with 15 percent in 1992.
In Rotterdam, the authorities are still studying the issue of soft drug taking.
"Of course there is a problem and (we wish) to prevent new shops from finding a place," says Margreet Enceaux, spokeswoman for Rotterdam city council.
The Netherlands' second largest city has launched a study into the issue, but currently has its hands full tackling the problems of hard drug trafficking.
"We first have to deal with the hard drugs. The problems are growing. We are one of the main transfer points in northern Europe," Enceaux says.

"Here drugs are cheaper and often purer than elsewhere. If you buy one gramme (of cocaine) in France, it costs about three times as much as in Rotterdam," says Anne Geelof of the Rotterdam police department.
Geelof says Rotterdam is beginning to reap the benefits of the police clampdown on drugs trafficking and drugs tourism which started late last year.
"We tried to arrest many French, Belgians and Germans and we see now that not so many of them are coming to Rotterdam," Geelof says.
GREATER SUCCESS AT STOPPING DRUG IMPORTS AT SOURCE
The police also claim greater success in stopping drugs imports at source.
Last month, police raided a container ship in Rotterdam and made a record haul of 3,000 litres of chemicals used in manufacturing the designer drug ecstasy.
But an estimated 90,000 litres was already thought to have got through, enough to manufacture 90 million ecstasy pills.
In Amsterdam, too, the attitude towards hard drugs is tough and getting tougher.
Police closed the city's chic Mazzo disco in December after a raid uncovered ecstasy tablets being peddled on the premises.
Police and local nightclubs are now in talks to launch a joint programme to wipe out drugs in clubs.

But while the tougher line on drugs of all kinds has gone some way to appeasing the Netherlands' European counterparts -- epitomised by the public kiss-and-make-up between French and Dutch justice ministers at a recent Euro-summit -- the Dutch determination to tolerate soft drugs is bound to continue to cause controversy.
